subtopics.title: Islamabad MoU and the 14-point roadmap
subtopics.summary: The United States and Iran signed the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding in June 2026. The MoU is an interim diplomatic framework rather than a permanent peace treaty. It provides for an immediate ceasefire, a 60-day negotiation process, and phased steps on Strait of Hormuz traffic and sanctions.
facts: US and Iran signed the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in June 2026.
The Islamabad MoU is an Interim Diplomatic Framework, not a Permanent Peace Treaty.
Immediate ceasefire followed by a 60-day negotiation process.
Negotiations cover nuclear issues, regional security and sanctions relief.
The proposed arrangement includes a 14-point MoU roadmap.
Strait of Hormuz to reopen and commercial maritime traffic restored during the 60-day window.
Phased sanctions relief and easing of restrictions on Iranian oil exports.
Iran to downblend highly enriched uranium under IAEA supervision.
Iran to refrain from nuclear weapon development.
Proposal for a UN Security Council-backed Comprehensive Agreement after negotiations conclude.

subtopics.title: Iran-U.S. nuclear diplomacy: JCPOA to 2018
subtopics.summary: The Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (2015) set limits on Iran's nuclear programme in return for easing of international sanctions. The United States withdrew from the nuclear agreement in 2018. Iran then gradually scaled back its compliance with several JCPOA commitments.
facts: JCPOA was concluded in 2015 between Iran and the P5+1 countries.
Iran agreed to restrict uranium enrichment activities under the JCPOA.
Iran agreed to reduce its nuclear stockpiles under the JCPOA.
Iran agreed to permit enhanced international inspections under the JCPOA.
In return, international economic and financial sanctions on Iran were eased.
In 2018, the United States withdrew from the nuclear agreement.
Iran gradually scaled back compliance with several JCPOA commitments.
The scaled-back commitments related mainly to uranium enrichment and nuclear monitoring.

subtopics.title: Three strategic pillars and their impact
subtopics.summary: The booklet groups the accord's benefits into three pillars: regional stability, energy markets and economic development. Reopening the Strait of Hormuz is expected to cut freight and insurance costs. Persistent regional tensions and doubts about the 60-day timeline are the main challenges.
facts: Pillar 1: Strengthening regional stability, through reduced conflict risks and an improved security environment.
Pillar 2: Energy market benefits, including reduced oil price volatility.
Pillar 3: Economic developmental gains, including stimulated trade and investment.
Reopening the Strait of Hormuz reduces freight and insurance costs.
Lower crude oil prices would lower India's inflationary pressures and current account deficit.
Reintegration of Iran boosts the Chabahar Port and the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC).
Experts doubt a comprehensive settlement can be concluded within the two-month timeframe.
Tensions between Israel and Hezbollah, and Iranian regional proxies, continue to persist.

subtopics.title: IAEA: origins, objectives and leadership
subtopics.summary: The International Atomic Energy Agency was founded in 1957 and is an intergovernmental organization. It grew out of the 1953 Atoms for Peace speech by US President Dwight D. Eisenhower. Its objectives are to promote peaceful use of nuclear energy and to inhibit its use for military purposes.
facts: IAEA was founded in 1957.
IAEA was born out of US President Dwight D. Eisenhower's Atoms for Peace speech to the UNGA in 1953.
IAEA is an intergovernmental organization.
Objective: to promote peaceful use of nuclear energy.
Objective: to inhibit use of nuclear energy for any military purpose.
IAEA was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2005.
Head of the IAEA: Rafael Grossi.
Headquarters of the IAEA: Vienna, Austria.

subtopics.title: Visit Outcomes
subtopics.summary: Myanmar's President Min Aung Hlaing made a five-day official visit to India, his first since the political transition in Myanmar. The talks produced commitments on border security, a currency settlement framework, connectivity projects and scholarships. Both sides reaffirmed the Kaladan project and agreed to expedite the Trilateral Highway.
facts: Myanmar's President Min Aung Hlaing made a five-day official visit to India.
It was his first visit to India since the political transition in Myanmar.
Myanmar assured India that its territory would not be used by anti-India insurgent groups near the border.
Both sides agreed to promote greater use of the Rupee-Kyat settlement framework, operational since 2024.
Both countries reaffirmed their commitment to complete the Kaladan project at the earliest.
Efforts were announced to expedite the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway.
India increased the number of Mekong-Ganga ICCR scholarships for Myanmar students from 36 to 100.

subtopics.title: Historical Background
subtopics.summary: Much of India's North-East was under Burmese occupation until the Treaty of Yandaboo, signed in 1826 to end the Anglo-Burmese War of 1824-1826. The treaty established the current India-Myanmar boundary. General Sir Archibald Campbell signed it on behalf of the British.
facts: Much of India's North-East Region was under Burmese occupation until the Treaty of Yandaboo.
The Treaty of Yandaboo was signed in 1826.
The treaty ended the Anglo-Burmese War of 1824-1826.
General Sir Archibald Campbell signed the treaty on behalf of the British.
The treaty established the current India-Myanmar boundary.

subtopics.title: Strategic Importance and Relations
subtopics.summary: Myanmar is India's only ASEAN neighbour connected through both land and maritime boundaries, which makes it a geographic bridge to Southeast Asia. Cooperation with Myanmar is important for tackling insurgency, narcotics trafficking and cross-border crime. Ties are framed within India's Act East and Neighbourhood First policies.
facts: Myanmar is India's only ASEAN neighbour connected through both land and maritime boundaries.
India shares a border of 1643 km with Myanmar across Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur and Mizoram.
India and Myanmar share a maritime boundary in the Bay of Bengal.
Myanmar acts as a bridge between South Asia and South-East Asia.
India and Myanmar signed a Treaty of Friendship in 1951.
Cooperation with Myanmar is critical for tackling insurgency, narcotics trafficking, illegal arms smuggling and cross-border crime.
Myanmar is a member of BIMSTEC, a SAARC observer and part of the Mekong-Ganga Cooperation.
Bilateral trade is conducted under the ASEAN-India Trade in Goods Agreement (AITIGA).

subtopics.title: Connectivity Projects
subtopics.summary: The Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project links Kolkata with Sittwe Seaport in Rakhine, Myanmar, via the Bay of Bengal. The India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway runs from Moreh in Manipur through Myanmar to Mae Sot in Thailand. Both projects featured in the outcomes of the visit.
facts: The Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project links Kolkata with Sittwe Seaport in Rakhine, Myanmar.
The Kaladan project links India and Myanmar via the Bay of Bengal.
The India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway is 1,360 km long.
The Trilateral Highway starts from Moreh in Manipur.
The Trilateral Highway passes through Myanmar before reaching Mae Sot in Thailand.
Both countries reaffirmed commitment to complete Kaladan at the earliest, and efforts to expedite the Trilateral Highway were announced.

subtopics.title: Myanmar's Political Background
subtopics.summary: The military seized power in Myanmar on February 1, 2021, after alleging huge irregularities in the November parliamentary polls. Aung San Suu Kyi and other civilian leaders were taken into custody, and a one-year state of emergency was declared. The NLD had won landslide victories in 2015 and 2020.
facts: The military seized power on February 1, 2021.
The military alleged huge irregularities in the November parliamentary polls.
The army declared a one-year state of emergency.
Myint Swe, a former general and the vice president, was to become acting president.
Aung San Suu Kyi and other civilian leaders were taken into custody hours before parliament was due to convene.
Internet and mobile phone communications were severely restricted and all banks were closed nationwide.

topics.title: PM Modi Became India's Longest Continuously Serving Elected PM

subtopics.title: Modi's Record-Breaking Continuous Tenure
subtopics.summary: Narendra Modi became India's longest continuously serving elected Prime Minister after completing 4,399 consecutive days in office since 26 May 2014. He surpassed the uninterrupted tenure record held by Jawaharlal Nehru. The milestone is the longest uninterrupted period served by a democratically elected Prime Minister in independent India.
facts: Modi completed 4,399 consecutive days in office.
He has been in office since 26 May 2014.
He surpassed the uninterrupted tenure record held by Jawaharlal Nehru.
It is the longest uninterrupted period served by a democratically elected PM in independent India.
Nehru's overall tenure as Prime Minister lasted approximately 6,131 days.
Nehru's cumulative tenure includes his time as PM of the Interim Government.
Gulzari Lal Nanda was interim PM on both occasions.

subtopics.title: Constitutional Position of the Prime Minister
subtopics.summary: The Prime Minister is the head of the Union Government and the leader of the Council of Ministers. The booklet describes the PM as head of the executive, chairperson of the Union Cabinet and chief coordinator of government policy and administration. Article 74 provides for a Council of Ministers headed by the PM to aid and advise the President, while Article 75 deals with the appointment, tenure and responsibilities of the PM and the Council of Ministers.
facts: The PM is the Head of the Executive.
The PM is the Chairperson of the Union Cabinet.
The PM is Head of the Union Government and leader of the Council of Ministers.
The PM is the chief coordinator of government policy and administration.
If a member of Lok Sabha, the PM is its leader.
Article 74 provides for a Council of Ministers headed by the PM to aid and advise the President.
Article 75 deals with the appointment, tenure and responsibilities of the PM and Council of Ministers.
Article 163 establishes State Councils of Ministers led by the Chief Minister to aid and advise the Governor.

subtopics.title: Appointment, Tenure and the Council of Ministers
subtopics.summary: The President appoints the PM but is not free in the selection, and normally invites the leader of the majority party in the Lok Sabha to form the government. If no single party has a clear majority, the President invites a person likely to command support of two or more parties that make up a Lok Sabha majority. The PM holds office during the pleasure of the President but cannot be dismissed while enjoying majority support in the Lok Sabha. Rules for the Council of Ministers include a 15% size cap and a six-month limit for ministers who are not in Parliament.
facts: The President normally invites the leader of the majority party to form the government.
If no single party has a clear majority, the President invites a person who can command support of two or more parties forming a Lok Sabha majority.
The PM is normally the leader of the majority party in the Lok Sabha.
Some Members of the Rajya Sabha have been made Prime Minister.
The PM holds office during the pleasure of the President.
The President cannot dismiss the PM while he enjoys majority support in the Lok Sabha.
If the PM loses the confidence of the Lok Sabha, he must resign or the President can dismiss him.
The salary and allowances of the PM are determined by Parliament.
The size of the Council of Ministers cannot exceed 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha (91st Amendment, 2003).
A minister who is not in Parliament for six months will lose their position.
Article 88 allows ministers to take part in both Houses but does not guarantee them voting rights.

subtopics.title: Modi's Firsts and Records in Context
subtopics.summary: Modi is the first Indian PM born after 15 August 1947 and the longest-serving PM from outside the Indian National Congress. He is among the few Indian PMs to secure three consecutive electoral mandates at the Union level. In 2014, the BJP-led NDA won an absolute majority of 336 out of 543 Lok Sabha seats, which the booklet calls the first Non-Congress single party majority government.
facts: Modi is the first Indian PM born after 15 August 1947.
Modi is the longest-serving PM from outside the Indian National Congress.
Modi is among the few Indian PMs to secure 3 consecutive electoral mandates at the Union level.
Modi is the 3rd PM after Nehru and Indira Gandhi to serve 3 terms.
In 2014, the BJP-led NDA got an absolute majority of 336 out of 543 Lok Sabha seats.
The 2014 government is described as the first Non-Congress single party majority government.
The BJP became the first party since 1984 to get a majority in the Lok Sabha.
Morarji Desai was India's first Non-Congress PM and its oldest PM at 81 years.
Rajiv Gandhi was India's youngest PM at 40 years.
V.P. Singh was the first PM to leave office following a no-confidence vote.

topics.title: Passport Is Not Proof of Citizenship

subtopics.title: Passport as a Travel Document
subtopics.summary: The Ministry of External Affairs clarified on Passport Seva Divas (June 24) that an Indian Passport is primarily a Travel Document, not conclusive proof of citizenship. Courts treat it as strong evidence of nationality, while citizenship is decided on constitutional criteria. Section 20 of the Passports Act, 1967 allows passports to be issued to non-citizens in the public interest.
facts: Ministry of External Affairs clarified this on Passport Seva Divas (June 24)
Indian Passport is primarily a Travel Document
Passport is Strong Evidence of Nationality but not Conclusive Proof of Citizenship in legal disputes
Maneka Gandhi vs Union of India (1978): passport recognised as a Travel Document subject to constitutional protections
State of Andhra Pradesh vs Abdul Khader (1962): Supreme Court held passport as supporting evidence
Citizenship depends on constitutional criteria, not on the passport
Section 20, Passports Act 1967: Central Government may issue passports to non-citizens in public interest
Section 20 has been used for stateless persons, certain Tibetan refugees and Sri Lankan Tamil refugees needing international travel

subtopics.title: Identity Documents vs Citizenship
subtopics.summary: No single universal document conclusively proves Indian citizenship. Aadhaar shows identity and residence, a Voter ID shows electoral eligibility, and a Ration Card shows residence and welfare eligibility. Inclusion in the electoral roll creates a presumption of citizenship that only due legal process can displace.
facts: No single universal document conclusively proves Indian citizenship
Aadhaar: proof of identity and residence, not citizenship
Voter ID: establishes electoral eligibility, not citizenship
Ration Card: indicates residence and eligibility for welfare benefits, not citizenship
Lal Babu Hussein vs Electoral Registration Officer (1995): inclusion in electoral roll creates a presumption of citizenship
That presumption can be displaced only through due legal process
Citizenship Certificate is issued only to persons acquiring citizenship through registration or naturalisation
Persons acquiring citizenship by birth or descent do not receive a Citizenship Certificate
Sarbananda Sonowal vs Union of India (2005): burden of proving Indian citizenship lies on the person claiming it
Deletion from electoral roll does not amount to loss of citizenship

subtopics.title: Constitution and Citizenship Act, 1955
subtopics.summary: Articles 5 to 11 of the Constitution decided who became a citizen at the commencement on January 26, 1950. The Citizenship Act, 1955 governs acquisition and loss of citizenship, and has been amended six times since 1986. India does not permit dual citizenship.
facts: Articles 5 to 11 (Part 2) of the Constitution deal with citizenship at commencement (January 26, 1950)
Citizenship Act, 1955 governs acquisition and determination of citizenship
Ways to acquire citizenship: birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, incorporation of territory
Ways to lose citizenship: renunciation, termination, deprivation
Citizenship Act amended six times since 1986: 1986, 1992, 2003, 2005, 2015 and 2019
Citizenship (Amendment) Act 2003 shifted India's regime towards Jus Sanguinis and barred illegal migrants from acquiring citizenship
Citizenship Rules 2003 envisaged a National Register of Indian Citizens
Citizenship (Amendment) Act 2019 covers six communities from Pakistan, Afghanistan and Bangladesh who entered India on or before 31 December 2014
Citizenship (Amendment) Act 2019 exempts these communities from prosecution under the Foreigners Act, 1946 and the Passport Act, 1920 for illegal entry or overstaying
India does not permit dual citizenship

subtopics.title: Assam Accord and NRC
subtopics.summary: The Assam agitation of 1979-1985, led by AASU and AAGSP against illegal immigration, ended with a Memorandum of Settlement signed on August 15, 1985. Clause 6 of the Assam Accord mandates safeguards for Assamese identity. A committee headed by Justice (Retd) Biplab Kumar Sarma made 67 recommendations, of which 57 have been approved by the Assam Cabinet.
facts: Assam agitation years: 1979-1985
Agitation led by AASU and AAGSP against illegal immigration
Tripartite Memorandum of Settlement signed on August 15, 1985 by Central Government, Assam Government and agitation leaders
Clause 6 of Assam Accord: constitutional, legislative and administrative safeguards for Assamese identity and heritage
Committee headed by Justice (Retd) Biplab Kumar Sarma submitted 67 recommendations
57 recommendations approved by Assam Cabinet; 10 remain under discussion with Centre
AASU stands for All Assam Students' Union; AAGSP stands for All Assam Gana Sangram Parishad
Assam NRC: applicants had to establish links with legacy records predating 24 March 1971
NRC in Assam commenced in 2003 following an SC Order
NRC in Assam: 1951

topics.title: Draft Rules for VB-G RAM G Act 2025

subtopics.title: Objectives and Rural Infrastructure Linkage
subtopics.summary: VB-G RAM G is framed as a Rural Employment and Livelihood Programme that pairs wage employment with the creation of durable rural assets. Its objectives cover livelihood security, productive employment, rural infrastructure, climate resilience and local planning outcomes. Employment is linked to water conservation, rural connectivity and climate-resilient community assets, and planning is decentralised.
facts: VB-G RAM G stands for Viksit Bharat — Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin).
The Act is set to replace MGNREGA from July 2026.
It combines wage employment with creation of durable rural assets and infrastructure.
Objectives: livelihood security, productive employment, rural infrastructure, climate resilience, local planning outcomes.
Viksit Bharat National Rural Infrastructure Stack Programme links employment with infrastructure creation.
Assets created include water conservation assets, rural connectivity infrastructure, livelihood-supporting facilities and climate-resilient community assets.
Mandatory preparation of Viksit Gram Panchayat Plans.
Technology integration through the Yuktdhara Portal and integration with PM Gati Shakti.

subtopics.title: Employment Guarantee and Season Pause
subtopics.summary: Guaranteed wage employment per rural household rises from 100 days to 125 days a year. Wages must be paid within 15 days of work completion. States may declare a cumulative 60-day no-work period during peak sowing and harvesting seasons to prevent labour shortages in agriculture.
facts: Guaranteed wage employment increased from 100 days to 125 days annually per rural household.
Mandatory wage payment within 15 days of work completion.
Agricultural Season Pause: States may declare a cumulative 60-day No-Work Period.
The No-Work Period applies during peak sowing and harvesting seasons.
Objective of the pause: prevent labour shortages in agriculture and balance farm labour demand with employment guarantee objectives.

subtopics.title: Normative Allocation and Cost-Sharing
subtopics.summary: The Draft Rules replace MGNREGA's open-ended, demand-driven financing with a normative allocation formula based on devolution criteria recommended by the 16th Finance Commission. The formula weights GSDP distance at 42.5% and population at 17.5%, with other criteria at 10% each. Cost sharing is revised, with the Centre bearing 60% for general States and 90% for Northeastern and Himalayan States.
facts: Shift from MGNREGA's open-ended, demand-driven financing to a Normative Allocation Model.
Central allocations follow a Normative Allocation Formula based on devolution criteria recommended by the 16th Finance Commission.
The normative model promotes predictability in resource allocation.
GSDP distance carries 42.5% weightage and measures the gap between a State's per capita income and that of the wealthiest States.
Population carries 17.5% weightage and benefits States with larger populations and greater employment demand.
Other criteria carry 10% weightage each.
General States: Centre 60%, State 40%. Northeastern and Himalayan States: Centre 90%, State 10%.
Expenditure beyond the approved normative allocation must be fully financed by the concerned State Government.
Performance-linked funding begins from the 2nd year, based on timely wage payments, social audit compliance, public works completion rate and implementation efficiency.

subtopics.title: Governance and Transition
subtopics.summary: A 16-member National Level Steering Committee, chaired by the Union Rural Development Secretary, recommends State-wise allocations and monitors implementation. The Central Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Council, chaired by the Union Minister for Rural Development, advises the Centre on policy. e-KYC verified MGNREGA Job Cards remain valid during the transition period.
facts: National Level Steering Committee has 16 members.
The Steering Committee is chaired by the Union Rural Development Secretary.
Members include State Government representatives, NITI Aayog officials and representatives of relevant Union Ministries.
Steering Committee functions: recommend State-wise allocations, formulate operational standards, monitor implementation and compliance.
Central Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Council is chaired by the Union Minister for Rural Development.
The Council advises the Centre on policy implementation, reviews programme performance and facilitates coordination.
e-KYC verified MGNREGA Job Cards remain valid during the transition period.
Workers subsequently receive Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Cards under the new framework.

subtopics.title: Party System and Types of Parties
subtopics.summary: Political parties are groups of like-minded individuals who voluntarily organise to gain political power through constitutional means and promote the national interest. The booklet compares three party systems and gives examples of national and state parties in India. Recognised parties are allotted symbols reserved for their use in their jurisdiction.
facts: Political party: group of like-minded individuals who voluntarily organise to gain political power through constitutional means
Aim of parties: promote the national interest
Three party systems: one party (China), two party (USA), multi-party (India)
National parties (6) include AAP, BJP, INC, BSP and CPI-M among the examples
State parties include DMK, AIADMK, Telugu Desam, Shiv Sena, Asom Gana Parishad and Mizo National Front
Recognised national or state parties are allotted a symbol exclusively reserved for their use in their jurisdiction
The cockroach-as-symbol debate drew attention to the framework governing election symbols

subtopics.title: Criteria for Recognition
subtopics.summary: Parties are recognised as national or state parties on the basis of votes and seats won at general elections. The booklet sets separate criteria for each category, measured against valid votes polled and seats in the Lok Sabha or the legislative assembly.
facts: National party: secures 6% of valid votes in any 4 or more states at a general election to the LS or LA
National party: wins 4 LS seats from one or more states
National party: wins 2% of LS seats at a general election, from 3 states
National party: recognised as a state party in 4 states
State party: secures 6% of valid votes polled in the state at a GE to the LA and wins 2 LA seats
State party: wins 3% of LA seats or 3 LA seats, whichever is more
State party: secures 8% of total valid votes polled in the state at a GE to the LS or LA
State party: secures 6% of valid votes polled in the state at a GE to the LS and wins 1 LS seat from the state
State party: wins 1 LS seat for every 25 seats or fraction thereof allotted to the state

subtopics.title: 1968 Order: Reserved and Free Symbols
subtopics.summary: The Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968 was issued by the Election Commission and provides the legal framework for reservation and allotment of symbols. It separates reserved symbols, held exclusively by recognised parties, from free symbols, open to registered unrecognised parties and independent candidates.
facts: The Order was issued by the Election Commission of India in 1968
The Order provides the legal framework for reservation and allotment of election symbols
The Order covers registration, recognition and derecognition of parties
The Order covers classification of parties as national or state parties
The Order covers resolution of disputes arising from party splits and mergers
Reserved symbols are exclusively allotted to recognised national or state parties
Free symbols are available to registered unrecognised parties and independent candidates
Free symbols are allotted by the ECI from a notified list

subtopics.title: Party Splits and ECI's Role
subtopics.summary: The ECI is the sole authority to adjudicate disputes arising from splits within recognised parties and from mergers. It applies organisational and legislative tests before deciding whether one faction keeps the name and symbol, whether the other must register separately, or whether the symbol is frozen. Two Supreme Court decisions, Sadiq Ali (1972) and Kanhaiyalal Omar (1986), shape how these tests and the Order are applied.
facts: The ECI is the sole authority empowered to adjudicate disputes from splits within recognised parties and from mergers
Organisational wing test covers the party president, office bearers, and national and state executive members
Legislative wing test covers elected MPs, MLAs and MLCs (where applicable)
One faction may be recognised as the original party, retaining the name and symbol
The other faction must register separately under a different name and symbol
If neither faction shows a clear majority, ECI may freeze the original symbol and direct both groups to contest under new names and symbols
During the 1969 split of the Indian National Congress, ECI recognised Congress (O) and Congress (R)
If factions reunite later, they may approach ECI for restoration of the original name and symbol
Sadiq Ali (1972): majority support in both wings is crucial; legislative majority alone is not the sole criterion
Kanhaiyalal Omar (1986): the Symbols Order is a valid exercise of ECI's constitutional and statutory powers

topics.title: Telegram Ban under Section 69A of IT Act 2000

subtopics.title: Why Telegram was blocked
subtopics.summary: MeitY temporarily blocked Telegram in India under Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000, after criminal groups allegedly used its message-editing feature to target candidates of the NEET-UG 2026 Re-Examination. Fraudsters edited old messages after an exam had ended to create a false appearance of a pre-exam leak. The booklet also links rising cybercrime complaints to activities organised within Telegram groups.
facts: MeitY temporarily blocked Telegram in India under Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000.
Criminal groups allegedly used message editing to target and defraud NEET-UG 2026 Re-Examination candidates.
Fraudsters inserted fake exam papers into old messages after an exam had ended.
This retroactive editing created a false appearance of a pre-exam leak.
Hidden phone numbers and end-to-end encryption in secret chats make tracing malicious actors nearly impossible for investigators.
Telegram hosts marketplaces for renting bank accounts used in money laundering, extortion and illegal gambling.
Criminals use automated bots to distribute illegal content and coordinate large-scale activities with minimal manual effort.
Government data shows a sharp rise in official cybercrime complaints linked to activities in Telegram groups.

subtopics.title: Section 69A and the blocking procedure
subtopics.summary: Section 69A, introduced in 2008, lets the Central Government or an officer it specially authorises direct any government agency or intermediary to block public access to online information. The booklet lists six grounds for blocking. Requests are examined under the IT (Blocking Rules), 2009 through an Inter-Ministerial Review Mechanism. A Designated Committee evaluates necessity and legality, and interim directions may be issued in urgent situations.
facts: Section 69A was introduced in 2008.
The Central Government, or an officer it specially authorises, can direct blocking of online information.
Directions may go to any government agency or intermediary to block public access.
Six grounds: sovereignty and integrity of India; defence of India; security of State; friendly relations with foreign States; public order; prevention of incitement to cognisable offences.
Requests for blocking are examined under the IT (Blocking Rules), 2009.
The Blocking Rules use an Inter-Ministerial Review Mechanism.
A Designated Committee evaluates necessity and legality before the proposed action is implemented.
In urgent situations, Interim Blocking Directions may be issued before a Full Review, subject to subsequent examination.
The booklet calls Section 69A the primary legal mechanism for restricting access to digital content and online platforms.

subtopics.title: Constitutional basis and judicial review
subtopics.summary: Digital free speech is protected under Article 19(1)(a), while Article 19(2) allows reasonable restrictions. In Shreya Singhal vs Union of India (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A as a narrowly drawn provision and struck down the vague Section 66A. Later rulings from the Delhi and Karnataka High Courts dealt with disclosure of blocking orders and with the rights of foreign companies.
facts: Article 19(1)(a) protects digital free speech.
Article 19(2) allows the State to impose reasonable restrictions on free speech.
Shreya Singhal vs Union of India (2015): Supreme Court upheld Section 69A as a narrowly drawn provision.
The same judgment struck down the vague Section 66A.
Tanul Thakur vs Union of India (2022): Delhi High Court mandated disclosure of original blocking orders.
Tanul Thakur challenged the blanket confidentiality of Rule 16.
X Corp vs Union of India (2023): Karnataka High Court ruled that foreign companies cannot claim Article 19 rights to challenge blocking orders.

subtopics.title: Intermediary duties and Safe Harbour
subtopics.summary: The IT Rules, 2021 require intermediaries to appoint a Grievance Officer, a Chief Compliance Officer and a Nodal Contact Person, and to carry out monthly compliance reporting. Section 79(3)(b) allows certain ministries to issue takedown or blocking orders directly, implemented through the Sahyog Portal. Safe harbour under Section 79 protects intermediaries from liability for third-party content only while they meet their duties.
facts: IT Rules, 2021 require appointment of a Grievance Officer, Chief Compliance Officer and Nodal Contact Person.
Intermediaries must carry out monthly compliance and transparency reporting.
Unlawful content must be removed on government direction.
Section 79(3)(b) allows certain ministries to directly issue takedown or blocking orders.
Section 79(3)(b) orders are implemented through the Government's Sahyog Portal.
Section 79 grants online intermediaries immunity from liability for third-party content (safe harbour).
Safe harbour is available only if intermediaries exercise due diligence and comply with lawful government directions.
Failure to comply can lead to loss of safe harbour protection under Section 79.

subtopics.title: DPDP Act 2023 and privacy
subtopics.summary: The Supreme Court held in 2017 that privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 makes data fiduciaries accountable and lets platforms collect only the data needed for the services users opt for. The Act defines three roles, allows penalties of up to 250 crore on data fiduciaries, and sets rules such as a 72-hour breach notification and a 3-year retention limit for certain platforms.
facts: In 2017 the Supreme Court held that privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21.
A Data Fiduciary decides the purpose of processing personal data.
A Data Processor processes data on behalf of the Data Fiduciary.
A Data Principal is the individual whose data is processed.
Platforms may collect only the data required for their functioning and for services users have opted for.
A torch app does not need microphone or contact access.
Penalties of up to 250 crore can be imposed on Data Fiduciaries.
All data is categorised under three heads: general, sensitive and critical.
Data breaches must be notified to the Data Protection Board within 72 hours.
E-commerce, social media and gaming platforms must generally delete personal data after 3 years of user inactivity.

topics.title: WPI Base Year Revision and Introduction of PPI

subtopics.title: Wholesale Price Index (WPI) Basics
subtopics.summary: The Wholesale Price Index measures the average change in prices of goods traded at wholesale or producer level, before they reach final consumers. It is an important indicator of inflationary trends within the production and distribution chain. The Office of Economic Adviser compiles and releases it.
facts: Measures average change in prices of goods traded at wholesale or producer level
Captures prices before goods reach final consumers
Indicator of inflationary trends within the production and distribution chain
Compiled and released by the Office of Economic Adviser
Office of Economic Adviser works under the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade
Base year of the WPI before revision: 2011-12

subtopics.title: Base Year Revision and Major Reforms
subtopics.summary: The Government of India has approved revising the WPI base year from 2011-12 to 2022-23. The revised series changes the number of items, moves energy commodities to a different category, adopts a new weighting method and a new treatment of missing data. These changes aim to reflect the producer side of the economy more accurately.
facts: Government of India approved revision of WPI base year from 2011-12 to 2022-23
Number of items rises from 697 (WPI 2011-12) to 957 (WPI 2022-23)
Renewable energy inclusion adds Solar Power, Wind Energy and Nuclear Electricity as new components
Crude Petroleum and Natural Gas shifted from Primary Articles to Fuel and Power category
Revised weights are derived directly from Gross Value of Output
Earlier weights were based on Net Traded Value: Gross Value of Output + Imports - Exports
New missing-data approach: Targeted Mean Imputation
Previous missing-data approach: Carry-Forward Method, where missing prices were replaced by the last available price

subtopics.title: Producer Price Indices (PPIs)
subtopics.summary: For the first time, India will release dedicated Producer Price Indices with 2022-23 as base year. These indices track prices from the producer side and cover goods as well as services. Three indices are described: Output, Input and Service PPI.
facts: For the first time, dedicated PPIs will be released with 2022-23 as base year
Output PPI measures prices received by producers for goods and services they sell
Output PPI captures prices at factory gate or producer level, before taxes, trade margins and transportation costs
Output PPI reflects producer earnings and is an early indicator of future inflationary pressures
Input PPI measures prices paid by producers for inputs such as raw materials, intermediate goods and energy
Input PPI tracks production cost pressures and supply-side inflation
Service PPI measures prices received by service providers for services rendered
Services covered: banking, securities transactions, insurance, pension fund management, railways, air passenger transport and telecommunications

subtopics.title: WPI and PPI Compared
subtopics.summary: The PPI differs from the WPI in scope, focus, perspective and purpose. The WPI is primarily about goods and market-level wholesale prices, while the PPI covers goods and services and looks at producer revenue and input costs. The new PPIs are introduced alongside the revised WPI series.
facts: WPI scope: primarily goods; PPI scope: goods and services
WPI focus: wholesale price movements; PPI focus: producer-level price changes
WPI perspective: market-level wholesale prices; PPI perspective: producer revenue and input costs
WPI purpose: inflation monitoring; PPI purpose: comprehensive producer inflation analysis
New PPIs are introduced alongside the revised WPI series
Service PPI captures inflation trends in the services sector from the producer perspective

subtopics.title: 52nd G7 Summit 2026
subtopics.summary: The 52nd G7 Summit was held in Evian-les-Bains, France, under France's presidency, with the theme 'Forging New Partnerships and Rebuilding International Solidarity'. PM Modi participated in the Outreach Session, which marked India's 8th consecutive participation in the G7 Outreach Process. The rotating presidency is due to pass to the United States in 2027.
facts: 52nd G7 Summit held in Evian-les-Bains, France
Held under the French presidency
Theme 2026: Forging New Partnerships and Rebuilding International Solidarity
PM Modi participated in the 52nd G7 Summit Outreach Session
India's 8th consecutive participation in the G7 Outreach Process
Rotating presidency to hand over to the United States in 2027

subtopics.title: Evolution of the G7
subtopics.summary: The G7 was established in 1975 in response to global economic turbulence and an oil crisis, with six founding members. Canada joined in 1976, creating the G7, and Russia joined in 1998, leading to the formation of the G8. Russia's participation was suspended in 2014 following the annexation of Crimea, which restored the G7 format.
facts: Established in 1975 amid global economic turbulence and oil crisis
Founding members: France, West Germany, Italy, Japan, United Kingdom, United States
Canada joined in 1976, creating the G7
Russia joined in 1998, leading to the formation of the G8
Russia's participation suspended in 2014 after annexation of Crimea
Suspension restored the G7 format

subtopics.title: Membership and Structure
subtopics.summary: The G7 is an informal forum of some of the world's most advanced industrialised economies, serving as a platform for consultations on major economic, political and strategic issues. It has seven member countries, while the European Union takes part in deliberations without being counted as a formal member. Leadership of the group rotates annually among member states.
facts: Informal forum of the world's most advanced industrialised economies
Member countries: Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, UK, US
European Union participates in deliberations but is not a formal member
Accounts for around 10% of the world's population
Accounts for nearly 43% of global GDP
Leadership rotates annually among member states

subtopics.title: Pillars of G7 Influence
subtopics.summary: The booklet describes the G7's influence through several pillars, including shaping financial regulation, responding to crises, and coordinating on energy and geopolitical issues. The forum is also presented as a symbol of cooperation among major economies and as a catalyst for climate and humanitarian commitments. Its dialogue is described as a way to find common ground on complex global challenges.
facts: Summit discussions affect financial regulations and economic frameworks used worldwide
Enables a unified front when addressing economic crises, armed conflicts and public health emergencies
Leaders coordinate on energy insecurity and geopolitical instability
Collective decisions influence global trade policies, investment flows and economic recovery strategies
Primary symbol of cooperation among the world's major economies
Commitments serve as a catalyst for climate action and humanitarian assistance
Dialogue and coordination help find common ground on complex global challenges

subtopics.title: Origins and Core Objectives
subtopics.summary: The Quad grew out of humanitarian cooperation after the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami and its concept was championed by Shinzo Abe in 2007. The grouping was revitalised in 2017 amid concerns over China's expanding military and economic influence. It remains an informal strategic partnership of India, the United States, Japan and Australia.
facts: Quad foundations emerged through humanitarian cooperation after the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami.
The Quad concept was championed by former Japanese PM Shinzo Abe in 2007.
The grouping was revitalised in 2017 amid concerns over China's expanding military and economic influence.
Quad stands for Quadrilateral Security Dialogue.
Members: India, United States, Japan and Australia.
It is an informal strategic partnership, enabling cooperation without a formal military alliance.
Core objective: a Free, Open, Inclusive, Secure and Prosperous Indo-Pacific.
Principles: rule of law, freedom of navigation, territorial integrity, peaceful resolution of disputes.

subtopics.title: Maritime and Security Cooperation
subtopics.summary: Maritime cooperation is one strand of the 11th meeting's outcomes. The outcomes include a surveillance framework that uses tracking assets of all members and a partnership for near real-time maritime data. Security work also covers the Quad-at-Sea Ship Observer Mission, the Malabar Exercise and a counterterrorism tabletop exercise.
facts: Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration uses tracking and monitoring assets of all Quad members.
Immediate focus area of maritime surveillance: the Indian Ocean Region.
Maritime surveillance objective: strengthen maritime domain awareness and monitor illicit maritime activities.
Indo-Pacific Partnership for Maritime Domain Awareness enables near real-time maritime data sharing across regional waters.
Quad-at-Sea Ship Observer Mission was launched under the Wilmington Declaration.
Quad-at-Sea objective: improve naval coordination, enhance interoperability, counter illegal maritime activities.
India will host the next edition of the Quad-at-Sea Ship Observer Mission.
Malabar Exercise is an annual multilateral naval exercise of Quad members.
Quad Counterterrorism Tabletop Exercise focuses on state-sponsored terrorism, UAV threats and joint crisis response planning; to be hosted by Australia in 2026.

subtopics.title: Economic Security and Emerging Technologies
subtopics.summary: The Quad's economic agenda centres on critical minerals, energy security and supply-chain resilience. Its infrastructure and technology work covers Pacific island connectivity, digital identity interoperability and AI-driven agriculture. Several initiatives aim to diversify sources beyond dominant suppliers.
facts: Quad Critical Minerals Initiative Framework coordinates investments and policies on mining, processing and recycling of critical minerals.
Critical minerals significance: reduce supply-chain vulnerabilities and diversify sources beyond dominant suppliers.
Indo-Pacific Energy Security Initiative launched a Joint Regional Energy Roadmap with commitment of over USD 25 million.
Energy focus areas: energy technology integration, supply chain resilience and market risk assessment.
Pacific Island Infrastructure Outreach is a collaboration with Fiji.
Outreach goals: connect all Pacific Island Forum countries through resilient undersea cable networks and modernise port infrastructure.
Outreach target: completion by 2026.
Digital Identity Interoperability involves developing a technical 'Translation Guide' for digital identity systems.
AI-ENGAGE Initiative aims to enhance agricultural productivity and food security across the Indo-Pacific.

subtopics.title: Significance for India and the Global Order
subtopics.summary: The Quad is presented as a strategic counterbalance that opposes unilateral attempts to alter the status quo. For India, it helps balance China's growing maritime presence, improve monitoring of maritime activity and attract investment. Its technology and supply-chain work also supports diversification under the China+1 strategy.
facts: Strategic counterbalance: supports freedom of navigation and opposes unilateral attempts to alter the status quo.
Supply-chain resilience supports diversification under the China+1 strategy.
Technology cooperation covers AI, cybersecurity, 5G/6G, Open RAN networks and secure digital infrastructure.
Quad provides regional public goods: disaster relief, health security, infrastructure support and capacity building.
For India, the Quad balances China's growing maritime presence and String of Pearls strategy in the Indian Ocean.
For India, the Quad preserves strategic autonomy without entering a formal military alliance.
For India, the Quad enhances monitoring of maritime activities and detection of illegal fishing and grey-zone tactics.
Blue Dot Network and the Supply Chain Resilience Initiative helped India attract foreign investment and integrate into global value chains.

subtopics.title: Ethanol and E85 Basics
subtopics.summary: Ethanol is a highly purified alcohol that is blended with petrol to make transport fuel. E85 is a blend of 85% ethanol and 15% petrol, and it can be used only in Flex-Fuel Vehicles. The Ethanol Blending Programme is overseen by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.
facts: Ethanol is highly purified alcohol with approximately 99.9% purity.
Major feedstocks for ethanol are sugarcane, maize, wheat and other sugar- and starch-rich crops.
Ethanol blending means mixing ethanol with petrol to create fuel for internal combustion engines.
E85 is a fuel blend of 85% ethanol and 15% petrol (gasoline).
E85 can be used only in Flex-Fuel Vehicles built to run on varying ethanol-petrol blends.
The Ethanol Blending Programme was piloted in 2003 and later expanded under the National Policy on Biofuels (2018).
The Ethanol Blending Programme targeted 20% ethanol blending (E20) by 2030, achieved in 2025.
Nodal ministry for the Ethanol Blending Programme is the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.
Ethanol and biodiesel are the most common biofuels.

subtopics.title: Benefits of Ethanol Blending
subtopics.summary: Ethanol blending is promoted for energy security, environmental gains and farm incomes. It cuts crude oil imports and gives a buffer against price shocks. It also turns agro-waste into fuel and encourages maize over sugarcane.
facts: Import reduction: ethanol cuts India's dependence on crude oil imports.
Blending buffer: ethanol stockpiles give flexibility for price stabilisation against crude oil shocks.
Lifecycle emissions: 2G ethanol reduces GHG emissions by over 50% compared to petrol.
Agro-waste utilisation: stubble, dung and biomass are converted into fuel, supporting a circular economy.
Farmer income: since 2014, farmers have earned about 21 lakh crore through ethanol procurement transfers.
Crop diversification: promotes maize cultivation and reduces over-dependence on sugarcane.
Objectives include reducing crude oil imports and providing assured markets for farmers.

subtopics.title: Concerns with Ethanol Blending
subtopics.summary: A survey finds that many petrol vehicle owners report reduced mileage and higher maintenance costs. Water-intensive sugarcane and land degradation are listed as environmental concerns. Diverting rice and corn for ethanol raises food-versus-fuel questions.
facts: A survey finds 67% of petrol vehicle owners report reduced mileage and higher maintenance costs.
Sugarcane has a high water requirement of 60-70 tonnes per tonne.
Water-intensive sugarcane drives groundwater depletion.
Unsustainable farming causes degradation of nearly 30% of India's land.
Diverting rice and corn for ethanol production raises food-versus-fuel concerns.
Imports and food security concerns are listed as a further issue.

subtopics.title: Biofuel Generations
subtopics.summary: Biofuels are grouped into generations by their feedstock and their carbon impact. First-generation fuels use edible items, while second-generation fuels use leftovers of food crops. Third- and fourth-generation fuels use microorganisms and genetically engineered crops.
facts: 1st generation biofuel is made from edible items such as sugar, corn and starch, and has high carbon content.
2nd generation biofuel is made from leftovers of food crops such as rice husk and wood chips.
2nd generation biofuel has lower greenhouse gas content than 1st generation biofuel.
3rd generation biofuel is produced using microorganisms such as algae and is carbon neutral.
4th generation biofuel is made from genetically engineered crops and is carbon negative.
The National Policy on Biofuels includes production of 2G ethanol as a key element.
A 2G ethanol project is located at Panipat, Haryana.

subtopics.title: Policies, Schemes and Alliances
subtopics.summary: The National Policy on Biofuels aims to reduce import dependence through blending. Schemes such as PM JI-VAN Yojana and GOBAR-DHAN support 2G ethanol and waste-to-energy conversion. India also launched the Global Biofuels Alliance with partner countries in 2023.
facts: National Policy on Biofuels (2018) aims to reduce import dependence by blending bioethanol, biodiesel and Bio-CNG.
PM JI-VAN Yojana (2019) gives financial assistance for developing 2G ethanol from surplus biomass and agricultural waste.
GOBAR-DHAN Scheme (2018) converts cattle dung and solid waste into compost, biogas and bio-CNG.
GOBAR-DHAN was launched under the Swachh Bharat Mission (Gramin).
Repurpose Used Cooking Oil (RUCO) was launched by FSSAI to convert used cooking oil into biodiesel.
BioE3 Policy aims to set up Bio-Foundries that produce biotechnology-developed feedstock and catalysts.
The Cabinet approved a Hydrogen Mission on 04 January 2023 with an outlay of Rs. 19,744 crore.
The Global Biofuels Alliance was launched in 2023 by India on the sidelines of the G20 Summit in New Delhi.
The Global Biofuels Alliance aims to facilitate global biofuel trade and provide technical support for national programmes.

subtopics.title: World Environment Day and UNEP
subtopics.summary: World Environment Day is celebrated every year on June 5 and was established in 1972 to coincide with the opening of the Stockholm Conference on Human Environment. It is organised by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), which is based in Nairobi, Kenya. The 2026 edition carried the theme 'Inspired by Nature. For Climate. For Our Future.' and named Azerbaijan as Global Host.
facts: World Environment Day is celebrated on June 5 every year.
Established in 1972 to coincide with the opening of the Stockholm Conference on Human Environment.
Celebrated in 1973 with the theme 'Only One Earth'.
Organised by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP).
UNEP was founded in 1972 and is based in Nairobi, Kenya.
Purpose: raise awareness and drive global action on pressing environmental issues.
WED 2026 theme: 'Inspired by Nature. For Climate. For Our Future.'
Azerbaijan was named Global Host for World Environment Day 2026.

subtopics.title: Global Climate Finance and the Tropical Forest Facility
subtopics.summary: The New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG) on climate finance was formally established at COP29 in Baku. It sets a target to scale up climate funding for developing nations to at least $1.3 trillion per year by 2035, with developed nations leading the mobilisation of at least $300 billion annually. The Tropical Forest Forever Facility was officially launched at COP30 in Belem, Brazil, to make standing forests more valuable than cleared land.
facts: The NCQG on climate finance was formally established at COP29 in Baku.
Target: scale up climate funding to developing nations to at least $1.3 trillion per year by 2035.
Developed nations agreed to lead mobilisation of at least $300 billion annually by 2035.
The Baku-Belem Roadmap to 1.3T designed an institutional mechanism spanning the Azerbaijan and Brazil Presidencies.
The Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF) was officially launched at COP30 in Belem, Brazil.
COP30 in Belem is widely termed the 'Amazon Forest COP'.
TFFF makes standing, living tropical forests more economically valuable than cleared land.
TFFF directly addresses the financial drivers of deforestation.

subtopics.title: India's Climate Targets and the Solar Alliance
subtopics.summary: India's Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) set targets on emissions intensity, non-fossil power capacity and carbon sinks, and the updated NDC submitted in 2022 raised the 2030 goals. The status column shows that the 2030 non-fossil target had reached 52.57% by February 2026. The International Solar Alliance, launched by India and France in 2015, was officially established in December 2017.
facts: First NDC (submitted 2015): cut emissions intensity of GDP by 33-35% from 2005 levels by 2030.
Updated NDC (submitted 2022): cut emissions intensity of GDP by 45% by 2030.
Non-fossil fuel based installed electric power capacity: 40% by 2030 (first NDC), 50% (updated NDC).
First NDC: additional carbon sink of 2.5-3 billion tonnes CO2 equivalent by 2030 through forest and tree cover.
Status: 36% reduction in emissions intensity achieved by 2020.
Status: 52.57% non-fossil fuel based installed capacity achieved by February 2026.
Status: 2.29 billion tonnes CO2 equivalent additional carbon sink achieved by 2021.
International Solar Alliance (ISA) jointly launched by India and France in 2015 on the sidelines of COP-21 in Paris.
ISA was officially established on 6 December 2017, on the entry into force of the Framework Agreement.
ISA covers solar resource-rich states lying fully or partially between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn.

subtopics.title: Forest, Wetland and Restoration Drives in India
subtopics.summary: India runs several land-based programmes to expand and protect green cover. The National Mission for Green India aims to add forest and tree cover on 5 million hectares and improve quality on another 5 million hectares. The Aravalli Green Wall is a planned 1,400 km by 5 km green belt from Porbandar (Gujarat) to Panipat (Haryana), intended to halt desertification from the Thar Desert.
facts: National Mission for Green India (2014) is one of 8 missions under the National Action Plan on Climate Change.
Green India Mission: increase forest/tree cover on 5 million hectares and improve quality on another 5 million hectares.
CAMPA funds promote afforestation and regeneration on waste, vacant and barren lands.
India expanded its Ramsar Site count to 100 as of now.
India ranks 3rd globally in net forest area gain over the past 15 years.
Project Tiger was launched in 1973 and Project Elephant in 1992.
MISHTI (Mangrove Initiative for Shoreline Habitats and Tangible Incomes) was announced in Union Budget 2023-24.
Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam: plant trees in memory of one's mother, linking emotional appeal with afforestation.
Aravalli Green Wall: 1,400 km x 5 km green belt from Porbandar (Gujarat) to Panipat (Haryana), inspired by Africa's Great Green Wall.
Aravalli purposes: halt desertification from the Thar Desert, restore degraded lands, improve air quality, biodiversity and climate resilience.

subtopics.title: Plastic Pollution, Cleanliness and Mission LiFE
subtopics.summary: Governments are negotiating an internationally legally binding instrument to end plastic pollution, through an Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee (INC) that has met in several cities since 2022. India's own efforts include the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan, launched in 2014, and Mission LiFE, first introduced in 2021. Industry and project-level initiatives such as the India Plastics Pact and Project REPLAN add to these efforts.
facts: Negotiators are developing an internationally legally binding instrument to end plastic pollution worldwide.
INC sessions: Punta del Este, Uruguay (2022); Paris, France (2023); Nairobi, Kenya (2023); Ottawa, Canada (May 2024).
Swachh Bharat Abhiyan was launched by the PM on Gandhi Jayanti, 2 October 2014, in New Delhi.
Swachh Bharat aimed for a 'Clean India' by 2 October 2019, the 150th birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi.
Bangladesh was the first country to ban thin plastic bags.
India Plastics Pact was launched in collaboration with the Confederation of Indian Industries (CII) and WWF.
Project REPLAN (REducing PLAstic in Nature) was launched by the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC).
REPLAN process: waste plastic is collected, cleaned, chopped, beaten and treated for softness.
Mission LiFE is an India-led global mass movement for protecting and preserving the environment.
Mission LiFE was first introduced in 2021 by PM Modi at COP26 in Glasgow, and aims to mobilise at least 1 billion people for 2022-2027.

subtopics.title: Economy, Logistics and Infrastructure
subtopics.summary: This group covers the April 2026 Index of Industrial Production (IIP) and the revised IIP series with 2022-23 as the new base year. It also covers the Logistics Port Performance Index for FY 2024-25 and the Zojila Tunnel on the Srinagar-Leh highway. IIP tracks short-term changes in industrial output, while the port index measures operational efficiency across cargo categories.
facts: IIP growth was 4.9% in April 2026, lower than 5.8% in April 2025.
Manufacturing, about 76% of IIP weight, expanded by 6.2% in April 2026.
Mining and quarrying contracted by more than 5% in April 2026.
The revised IIP series uses 2022-23 as base year, replacing 2011-12.
The revised series covers 1,042 products (earlier 839) and 463 item groups (earlier 407).
The revised series adds gas supply, water supply, sewerage and waste management activities.
Logistics Port Performance Index FY 2024-25: Paradip Port tops dry bulk, Sikka Port tops liquid bulk.
Port KPIs include vessel turnaround time, berth idle time, container dwell time and ship berth day output.
World Bank LPI: India's rank in the international shipments category improved from 44 to 22.
Zojila Tunnel is 13.15 km long, expected to be operational in 2028, and is part of a 33 km corridor.

subtopics.title: Environment, Energy and Space
subtopics.summary: The Western Ghats are set to get Ecologically Sensitive Area (ESA) notification, based largely on the Kasturirangan Committee's 2013 recommendations. The group also covers GRAPES-3, an India-Japan study of Earth's upper atmosphere, and the Energy Transition Index 2026 that ranks 120 countries.
facts: The government is set to notify ESAs in the Western Ghats, nearly 13 years after the first draft notification.
The notification is based largely on the K. Kasturirangan Committee (2013) recommendations.
The Kasturirangan approach covers about 56,000 sq km, about 37% of the Western Ghats.
The Western Ghats extend about 1,600 km along the west coast across six states and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
New mining and quarrying projects, thermal power plants and red category industries are restricted in ESAs.
GRAPES-3 is a cosmic-ray observatory at Ooty (Tamil Nadu), operated by the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research.
Researchers from India and Japan used GRAPES-3 to track real-time changes in Earth's upper atmosphere.
The Energy Transition Index 2026 (WEF and Accenture) assesses 120 countries; India moved up two places to 70th.
Six G20 countries are in the Energy Transition Index top 20: Germany 9th, France 10th, UK 11th, China 14th, Brazil 17th, USA 19th.

subtopics.title: Defence and Security
subtopics.summary: This group covers the SIPRI Yearbook 2026 on global militarisation and India's nuclear posture, and the two councils of India's Nuclear Command Authority. It also covers the S-400 and BrahMos systems, other major air and missile defence systems, and a leadership change at the Intelligence Bureau.
facts: SIPRI Yearbook 2026 ranks India as the 5th largest military spender after USA, China, Russia and Germany.
India's defence expenditure rose 8.9% to USD 92.1 billion in 2025.
India's nuclear arsenal reached 190 warheads, including 12 operationally deployed warheads.
The Political Council (chaired by the Prime Minister) is the sole body authorised to release nuclear weapons.
The Executive Council (chaired by the National Security Advisor) gives inputs to the Political Council and executes its directives.
India's nuclear milestones: 1974 Pokhran test, 1998 Operation Shakti, 2003 nuclear doctrine, 2008 NSG waiver.
India received the 4th squadron of S-400 Triumf from Russia; it is called Sudarshan in Indian service.
BrahMos is a supersonic cruise missile (Mach 2.8), jointly developed by DRDO and NPOM, and is conventional only; it was used in combat during Operation Sindoor.
Beaufort Castle, a Crusader-era fortress in southern Lebanon, was under Israeli control from the 1982 invasion until withdrawal in 2000.
Mahesh Dixit was appointed Director of the Intelligence Bureau for a 2-year tenure, succeeding Tapan Kumar Deka.

subtopics.title: Governance, Global Bodies and Peacekeeping
subtopics.summary: This group covers the FCRA Amendment Rules 2026, which tighten compliance for NGOs receiving foreign contributions. It also covers the FATF grey and black lists, the US-led Pax Silica initiative, and India's role in UN Peacekeeping.
facts: The Ministry of Home Affairs notified the FCRA Amendment Rules 2026; the FCRA Act 2010 replaced the 1976 Act.
NGOs must register under one or more of 5 approved categories: social, economic, educational, cultural and religious.
FCRA registration is valid for 5 years and must be renewed before expiry; foreign contributions cannot be transferred to other persons or organisations.
NGOs must utilise at least 75% of previously released foreign funds before receiving the next instalment.
FATF was created in 1989 by the G7 and is headquartered in Paris; Vivek Aggarwal was appointed its next Vice-President, the first time India will hold that post.
FATF grey list covers jurisdictions under increased monitoring; the black list covers high-risk jurisdictions.
Pax Silica is a US-led initiative for secure supply chains of AI-critical technologies; India joined in February 2026.
India is the 4th largest troop contributor to UN Peacekeeping and was the first country to deploy an all-women contingent (2007).
Major Abhilasha Barak received the UN Military Gender Advocate of the Year Award 2025 for work in UNIFIL, Lebanon.
The International Day of UN Peacekeepers is observed on 29 May; the 2026 theme is Invest in Peace.

subtopics.title: Awards, Rankings, Health and Heritage
subtopics.summary: This group covers the Padma Awards 2026 and their rules, the Pradhan Mantri Rashtriya Bal Puraskar and QS World University Rankings 2027. It also covers NFHS-6, International Day of Yoga 2026, the NCERT Dancing Girl restoration, and the proposed UNESCO nomination of Xuanzang's records.
facts: Padma Awards 2026 conferred 131 honours, including 5 Padma Vibhushan, 13 Padma Bhushan and 113 Padma Shri.
Padma Awards were instituted in 1954 and reorganised in 1955 into three categories.
The maximum is 120 awards per year; the cap excludes posthumous awards, foreign nationals, NRIs and OCIs.
Padma selection: recommendation by a committee chaired by the Cabinet Secretary, review by the PM, final approval by the President.
PM Rashtriya Bal Puraskar honoured 19 children (ages 5-18); it was created in 2018 by merging two earlier awards.
QS World University Rankings 2027: MIT retained the top position for the 15th consecutive year; IIT Delhi is India's highest-ranked institution at 118th.
NFHS-6 (2023-24): institutional births rose from 88.6% to 90.6%; stunting declined from 35.5% to 29.3%.
International Day of Yoga 2026 was the 12th edition, held on 21 June with the theme Yoga for Healthy Ageing.
NCERT restored the original image of the Dancing Girl figurine, a bronze statuette of about 4,500 years, excavated from Mohenjo-daro.
India and China are in advanced discussions to jointly nominate Xuanzang's 'Great Tang Records on the Western Regions' for UNESCO recognition.

quizzes.title: Islamabad MoU: practice set
quizzes.passage: In June 2026, the United States and Iran put their signatures to a memorandum known as the Islamabad MoU. The document is designed to halt open hostilities first, with an immediate ceasefire, and then to open a structured period of talks. Those talks are meant to cover three linked areas: nuclear questions, security in the wider region and relief from sanctions. Movement of commercial vessels through a key maritime route would be restored during this negotiation period, reassuring energy-importing countries. The background to the arrangement is a long dispute. An earlier agreement under which Iran accepted curbs on uranium enrichment and tighter inspections, in return for easing of international economic sanctions, was later abandoned by the United States. Iran responded by gradually reducing its compliance with the terms it had accepted. An international nuclear body, whose work includes promoting peaceful nuclear energy and blocking its military use, plays a central role in verifying any nuclear commitments. The accord also envisions a further comprehensive deal, backed by the United Nations Security Council, once negotiations are complete. Many observers remain cautious about whether the timelines can be met.

quizzes.passage: Supporters of the June 2026 understanding argue that its benefits would reach well beyond the two signatories. A safer environment in the region could lower the likelihood of direct military clashes and of confrontations fought through allied groups. Calmer conditions would also make oil supplies more dependable, and lower crude prices could ease the financial strain on countries that import most of their energy. Shipping costs could fall as insurers judge a critical route to be less risky, and investment could flow back into areas hit by conflict, helping to rebuild them. New trade links could also connect the markets of West and Central Asia, and the reintegration of the country could give a north-south transport corridor a fresh boost. Yet the outlook is not uniform. Some analysts doubt that the parties can settle every disputed issue in the time allowed. Meanwhile, tensions involving regional proxies remain. Balancing these hopes against those risks will shape whether the accord delivers lasting dividends for the wider region.

quizzes.passage: Myanmar's President, Min Aung Hlaing, recently completed a five-day official visit to India. It was his first visit since the political transition in Myanmar. Both sides also agreed to promote wider use of the Rupee-Kyat settlement framework, which is already in operation. The two countries reaffirmed their commitment to complete the Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project at the earliest. Efforts were also announced to expedite the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway. In education, India increased the number of ICCR scholarships available to Myanmar students. India seeks to enhance its ties with Myanmar in line with its Act East and Neighbourhood First policies. Myanmar's membership of several regional forums adds to its importance for India. Trade is an important part of this relationship, and the Kaladan project and the trilateral highway are central to plans for better physical links. quizzes.title: Modi's Milestone and the PM's Office
quizzes.passage: Narendra Modi has become India's longest continuously serving elected Prime Minister. This milestone was reached after he completed a long run of consecutive days in office, counted from the day he took office in 2014. The record he surpassed was an uninterrupted tenure record held by an earlier Prime Minister. The Prime Minister is the head of the Union Government and the leader of the Council of Ministers. He is normally the leader of the majority party in the Lok Sabha, and the President usually invites that leader to form the government. The Prime Minister is also the chief coordinator of government policy and administration, and he chairs the Union Cabinet. The Prime Minister's salary and allowances are decided by Parliament from time to time. Many Prime Ministers of India have held the office for very different lengths of time, and their careers are often compared through such records. Students preparing for examinations should understand both the constitutional rules that govern the office and the historical milestones attached to individual leaders. A clear grasp of appointment, tenure and the Council of Ministers helps in answering questions on the Prime Minister's position in the Union Government. Modi's record is a reminder that the office rests on the confidence of the Lok Sabha, not just on the length of a term.

quizzes.title: Council of Ministers and Key Rules
quizzes.passage: The Prime Minister is the head of the Union Government and leads the Council of Ministers. The Council is the body through which the government functions, and the Prime Minister acts as its chief coordinator for government policy and administration. Ministers are placed at different levels. Cabinet ministers are the senior members, and they often oversee key ministries such as Home Affairs, Finance and Defence. Ministers of State assist Cabinet ministers with specific functions, and some of them are given independent charge of a ministry. Deputy Ministers help Cabinet ministers or Ministers of State with administrative, political and parliamentary duties. This structure allows policy decisions to pass through senior leaders before they reach individual departments. The Constitution sets out the office of the Prime Minister, the Council of Ministers and the relationship between them and the President. At the state level, a similar arrangement exists, with a Chief Minister heading the council and advising the Governor. Students should learn which constitutional provisions govern these arrangements, and how the rules connect to the everyday working of the government.

quizzes.title: Passport and Proof of Citizenship
quizzes.passage: On Passport Seva Divas, observed on June 24, the Ministry of External Affairs set out what an Indian passport does and does not establish. Officials stressed that the document is primarily a travel document. The clarification came at a time when the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls was drawing attention and questions about who counts as a citizen were being raised. Courts have also been asked to examine how much weight a passport carries in legal disputes. The document is taken seriously as evidence of nationality, and the question of citizenship is decided against the criteria that the Constitution and the law provide. The law also lets the government act beyond citizens. A specific statutory provision authorises the Central Government to issue passports to non-citizens in the public interest. Stateless persons and certain refugees have been helped through this route when they needed to travel abroad, which shows that a passport can serve a practical purpose without proving citizenship. Ordinary documents follow the same logic. Many people carry identity cards, voter cards and ration cards in daily life, and each serves a particular purpose. Officials and courts look at what each document establishes and do not treat any one of them as a complete answer to the question of citizenship.

quizzes.title: Citizenship Law Framework
quizzes.passage: Indian citizenship is governed by a set of constitutional and statutory rules rather than by any single certificate. The Constitution, through a group of early articles, settled who became a citizen when the Republic began. Those articles were not meant to be read alone, because the detailed rules on how citizenship is gained and lost are set out in a separate law passed by Parliament. That law has changed over the decades. It has been amended several times since the 1980s, reflecting shifts in policy on illegal migration and on the status of migrants from neighbouring countries. Earlier changes altered the basis of citizenship, moving the regime toward a principle linked to parentage. Later changes eased the path for certain religious communities who had entered India from neighbouring countries before a fixed date. Some features of the system are firm. India does not allow a person to hold citizenship of another country alongside Indian citizenship. The law also sets out the circumstances in which citizenship can be lost. Officials and students alike should note that the rules fix who is a citizen, while documents only record or support that status. Keeping this distinction clear helps explain why a passport, a voter card or an identity number cannot by itself settle a citizenship question.

quizzes.passage:
The Union Government has released Draft Rules for the Viksit Bharat — Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act 2025, known as VB-G RAM G. The Act is set to replace the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act from July 2026. It is a Rural Employment and Livelihood Programme that combines wage employment with the creation of durable rural assets. Its objectives include enhancing livelihood security in rural areas, generating productive employment and improving climate resilience.

Employment generation is tied to building rural infrastructure, such as water conservation assets, rural connectivity and climate-resilient community assets. A national infrastructure programme carries this linkage forward. Rural planning is also decentralised and technology-based, and preparing Viksit Gram Panchayat Plans is mandatory.

The Act also allows a seasonal pause in work. States may declare a no-work period, which is meant to address labour shortages in agriculture during peak times. Guaranteed wage employment is to be paid promptly once the work is complete, and the rules fix a clear timeline for this payment.

Funding is changing too. The Draft Rules move away from the open-ended, demand-driven financing model of the earlier scheme. Central allocations will instead follow a normative formula based on devolution criteria, which is meant to bring predictability. Poorer states are to receive a larger share, and any spending beyond the approved allocation must be financed fully by the state.

quizzes.title: Allocation and Cost-Sharing Check
quizzes.passage:
The Draft Rules for the VB-G RAM G Act 2025 change how central money reaches states for rural employment. Under the earlier scheme, funding followed an open-ended, demand-driven model. Under the new approach, central allocations are set by a normative allocation formula. This formula is based on devolution criteria recommended by a finance commission and uses several weighted factors. One factor measures how far a state's per capita income lags behind that of the wealthiest states. Another reflects population and the employment demand that comes with it. The aim is to give economically weaker states a larger share and to promote equitable distribution.

Cost sharing is also revised. General States share costs with the Centre in one ratio, while Northeastern and Himalayan States receive a higher central share. Any expenditure beyond the approved normative allocation must be fully financed by the concerned state government. Central assistance is also linked to performance. From a later year of implementation, a portion of funds depends on timely wage payments, compliance with social audit requirements, completion of public works and overall implementation efficiency.

A National Level Steering Committee oversees these matters. It recommends state-wise allocations, formulates operational standards and monitors implementation and compliance.

quizzes.title: Party System and Symbols Practice
quizzes.passage: India's party system is built on groups of like-minded people who come together to gain political power through constitutional means. These groups organise voluntarily and their aim is to promote the national interest. Not every party enjoys the same status. Some are recognised as national parties and others as state parties, and recognition affects the symbols a party can use. A recognised party may be allotted a symbol for its own exclusive use within its area. Recognition depends on how a party performs at general elections, measured through vote shares and seats won in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies. Registered but unrecognised parties and independent candidates draw their symbols from a different pool. Problems arise when a recognised party splits. Each rival group may claim the party, and the question of who keeps its name and symbol becomes a formal dispute. Such disputes must be settled by a single authority. The framework covers how parties are registered and classified, how symbols are reserved and allotted, and how disputes are handled. Recent public debate about an unusual symbol brought fresh attention to these rules. Understanding this framework helps explain how elections are contested in India and why symbols matter to voters and parties alike.

quizzes.title: Party Splits Recall
quizzes.passage: Political parties are not always stable. A party may split when its members disagree, and each resulting group may claim to be the real party. When this happens, the question of who keeps the party's name and symbol becomes a dispute. Only one authority is empowered to decide such disputes, and it does not rely on a single measure of support. It looks at the backing a faction has among the party's office holders and executive members, and also at the support it has among the party's elected legislators. Majority support in both areas is treated as important. Historically, one such case involved a major national party that split, after which two new groups were recognised. The outcome of a dispute can take several forms. One faction may keep the name and symbol, while the other must register separately under a new name and a different symbol. Where neither faction can show that it commands a majority, the original symbol may be put on hold, and both groups are directed to contest under new names and symbols. Disputes arising from mergers of parties fall within the same authority's role. Courts have also been drawn into these matters, and their decisions have shaped how the tests are applied. The range of possible outcomes shows how much depends on the result of a dispute.
